title: Tonsillitis: Causes, Presentation, and Management
subject: Pathology
summary: Tonsillitis is inflammation of the tonsils, commonly caused by viral or bacterial infections. It presents with sore throat, difficulty swallowing, and fever. Prompt diagnosis and management are crucial to prevent complications, especially in low-resource settings where rheumatic fever is a concern.

sections.p: Tonsillitis is an acute or chronic inflammation of the palatine tonsils, typically presenting with a sore throat, dysphagia, and fever. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on history and physical examination findings.
b: Clinical diagnosis relies on visual inspection of the tonsils for redness, swelling, and exudates.
Differentiation between viral and bacterial causes is important for appropriate management, especially to prevent complications like acute rheumatic fever.

sections.p: Tonsillitis severity ranges from mild discomfort to severe pain with significant systemic symptoms. While formal staging systems are not universally applied, clinical assessment guides management decisions.
b: Mild: Sore throat, minimal systemic symptoms, able to swallow liquids.
Moderate: Significant sore throat, difficulty swallowing solids, fever, malaise.
Severe: Intense pain, inability to swallow even liquids, high fever, dehydration, potential airway compromise.
Recurrent tonsillitis: Multiple episodes (e.g., 7 in one year, 5 per year for two years, or 3 per year for three years).

sections.p: The majority of tonsillitis cases are viral, but bacterial infections, particularly Group A Streptococcus, are clinically significant due to potential complications.
b: Viral (most common): Adenovirus, Rhinovirus, Influenza virus, Parainfluenza virus, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), Herpes simplex virus.
Bacterial: Lancefield group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) is the most important cause due to risk of acute rheumatic fever.
Other bacterial: Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis.
Fungal: Candida species (rare, usually in immunocompromised individuals).

sections.p: Patients typically present with a constellation of symptoms and signs related to inflammation of the tonsils and surrounding pharynx.
b: Sore throat, often severe, making swallowing painful (odynophagia).
Difficulty swallowing (dysphagia).
Fever and chills.
Headache and malaise.
Referred ear pain.
On examination: Erythematous and swollen tonsils, often with white or yellow exudates (pus).
Tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy (swollen glands in the neck).
Halitosis (bad breath).

sections.p: Investigations aim to differentiate between viral and bacterial causes, especially Group A Streptococcus, and to rule out complications. Availability of tests varies greatly in low-resource settings.

t.b: To estimate the probability of Group A Streptococcus infection and guide antibiotic use. A high score suggests bacterial infection, a low score suggests viral. In low-resource settings, this guides empirical treatment when lab tests are unavailable.

To quickly detect Group A Streptococcus antigens from a throat swab. A positive result confirms bacterial infection; a negative result may require confirmation with culture if clinical suspicion is high.

t.a: Throat swab for culture and sensitivity
t.b: To definitively identify the causative bacteria and determine antibiotic susceptibility. This is the gold standard but results take 24-48 hours, which may delay treatment initiation. If unavailable, clinical judgment and Centor score guide treatment.
To assess for leukocytosis (elevated white blood cell count), which can suggest bacterial infection, or atypical lymphocytes in infectious mononucleosis. May not be readily available in all settings.

To diagnose infectious mononucleosis (Epstein-Barr virus) if suspected (e.g., prolonged fatigue, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly). Often unavailable in low-resource settings; diagnosis is then clinical.

sections.p: Certain signs indicate severe disease or developing complications, requiring urgent attention. These are particularly critical in settings with limited access to advanced care.
b: Airway obstruction: Stridor, severe difficulty breathing, drooling, muffled voice (hot potato voice).
Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy): Unilateral tonsillar swelling, deviation of the uvula, severe odynophagia, trismus (difficulty opening mouth).
Retropharyngeal abscess: Neck stiffness, torticollis, difficulty swallowing, respiratory distress.
Acute Rheumatic Fever: Develops 2-4 weeks after untreated Group A Streptococcus infection, leading to carditis, arthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules.
Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis: Presents with hematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, edema, 1-3 weeks after infection.
Sepsis: High fever, tachycardia, hypotension, altered mental status.

sections.p: Management focuses on treating the underlying cause, alleviating symptoms, and preventing complications. In low-resource settings, empirical treatment and supportive care are paramount.
b: Antibiotics (for bacterial tonsillitis): Penicillin V is the first-line treatment for Group A Streptococcus to prevent rheumatic fever. Amoxicillin is an alternative. Erythromycin or azithromycin for penicillin-allergic patients. Avoid ampicillin in suspected EBV due to rash risk.
Analgesia and antipyretics: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) or ibuprofen for pain and fever relief.
Hydration: Encourage oral fluid intake; intravenous fluids if dehydrated or unable to swallow.
Rest: Advise adequate rest.

Tonsillectomy: Considered for recurrent severe tonsillitis, chronic tonsillitis unresponsive to medical management, peritonsillar abscess not responding to drainage, or suspicion of malignancy (e.g., lymphoma).
Drainage of peritonsillar abscess: Incision and drainage or needle aspiration for quinsy.

sections.p: Follow-up ensures resolution of infection and monitors for complications. Prevention focuses on reducing transmission and prompt treatment of streptococcal infections.
b: Complete the full course of antibiotics, even if symptoms improve, to eradicate bacteria and prevent rheumatic fever.
Educate patients on symptoms of complications like rheumatic fever and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
Good hand hygiene to prevent spread of infection.
Avoid sharing utensils or drinks.
For recurrent tonsillitis, discuss indications for tonsillectomy.

sections.p: Several conditions can mimic tonsillitis, making accurate differentiation crucial for appropriate management.
b: Infectious mononucleosis (EBV): Often presents with exudative tonsillitis, fever, and lymphadenopathy, but typically involves posterior cervical nodes and prolonged fatigue. Splenomegaly and abnormal liver tests are common. Ampicillin should be avoided.
Peritonsillar abscess: A complication of tonsillitis, characterized by unilateral swelling, uvula deviation, and trismus.
Epiglottitis: A life-threatening condition causing severe sore throat, drooling, stridor, and tripod positioning, but usually without tonsillar exudates.
Diphtheria: Rare in vaccinated populations, but can cause a greyish pseudomembrane on tonsils and pharynx, associated with systemic toxicity.
Oral candidiasis (thrush): White patches on tonsils and oral mucosa, usually easily scraped off, seen in immunocompromised individuals.

sections.p: Interpreting diagnostic tests and clinical signs requires careful consideration, especially in resource-limited settings.
b: Negative RADT for Group A Streptococcus: A negative result does not completely rule out streptococcal infection, especially if clinical suspicion is high; a throat culture may be needed for confirmation.
Absence of exudates: Viral tonsillitis can present with exudates, and bacterial tonsillitis may not always have them, so exudates alone are not definitive for bacterial infection.
Normal white blood cell count: A normal FBC does not exclude bacterial tonsillitis, especially early in the infection.
Self-medication with antibiotics: Prior antibiotic use can lead to false-negative cultures or RADTs.

faq.q: What is the main difference between viral and bacterial tonsillitis?
faq.a: Viral tonsillitis is more common and usually self-limiting, while bacterial tonsillitis, especially due to Group A Streptococcus, carries a risk of serious complications like acute rheumatic fever if untreated.

faq.q: When should antibiotics be used for tonsillitis?
faq.a: Antibiotics are indicated for bacterial tonsillitis, primarily when Group A Streptococcus is suspected or confirmed, to prevent complications like acute rheumatic fever. They are not effective for viral tonsillitis.

faq.q: What are the signs of a peritonsillar abscess?
faq.a: A peritonsillar abscess typically presents with severe, unilateral sore throat, difficulty swallowing, a 'hot potato' voice, trismus (difficulty opening the mouth), and deviation of the uvula away from the affected side.

exam: A 7-year-old child presents with a 3-day history of sore throat, fever, and difficulty swallowing. On examination, you note erythematous tonsils with white exudates and tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy. What is your immediate diagnostic consideration, and what is the most critical complication you are trying to prevent in this setting? — Group A Streptococcus tonsillitis; preventing acute rheumatic fever.

You are working in a rural clinic with no access to laboratory tests. A patient presents with symptoms suggestive of tonsillitis. How would you decide whether to prescribe antibiotics, and what antibiotic would you choose? — Use clinical scoring systems like Centor/McIsaac criteria. If bacterial tonsillitis is highly suspected, prescribe empirical penicillin V (or amoxicillin) to cover Group A Streptococcus.

A 15-year-old presents with severe sore throat, fatigue, and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. You notice exudative tonsillitis. What specific investigation would you consider, and what drug should be avoided if this diagnosis is confirmed? — Consider a Monospot test or EBV serology for infectious mononucleosis; avoid ampicillin due to the risk of a generalized rash.

Describe the key features that would make you suspect a peritonsillar abscess as a complication of tonsillitis, and what is the initial management? — Key features include unilateral tonsillar swelling, uvula deviation, trismus, and a 'hot potato' voice. Initial management involves needle aspiration or incision and drainage, along with antibiotics.

A patient with recurrent tonsillitis is considering tonsillectomy. What are the generally accepted indications for tonsillectomy in this context? — Recurrent severe tonsillitis (e.g., 7 episodes in one year, 5 per year for two years, or 3 per year for three years), chronic tonsillitis unresponsive to medical management, or suspicion of malignancy.

Explain the pathophysiology of acute rheumatic fever following tonsillitis. — Acute rheumatic fever is a delayed, non-suppurative complication of Group A Streptococcus pharyngitis/tonsillitis, resulting from an autoimmune reaction where antibodies produced against streptococcal antigens cross-react with host tissues (molecular mimicry), particularly in the heart, joints, and brain.

A child treated for streptococcal tonsillitis develops facial puffiness and dark urine 2 weeks later. What complication should you suspect, and what is its underlying mechanism? — Suspect post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. It's an immune-complex mediated disease where antigen-antibody complexes deposit in the glomerular basement membrane, causing inflammation.
